strengths: Clear problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies and explains why standard group DRO fails when paired with the Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) loss—namely, the sensitivity of CTC loss to sequence length and acoustic/linguistic variations, leading to degenerate group weight concentration.

Sound and lightweight solution: CTC-DRO introduces two complementary and intuitive techniques—duration-matched batch loss aggregation and a smoothed weight update rule derived from a regularized objective—both of which add negligible computational overhead.

Solid empirical results: Across 5 diverse 6-language subsets and two strong foundation models (MMS and XLS-R), CTC-DRO consistently and substantially improves worst-case CER (up to 65.9% relative reduction) while simultaneously improving or maintaining average CER and LID accuracy, in stark contrast to standard group DRO which frequently degrades performance.

Informative analysis: The group weight trajectories (Figure 2) and ablation study (Table 4) provide clear visual and quantitative evidence of how the proposed smoothing and duration matching stabilize optimization and prevent single groups from dominating training.
weaknesses: Evaluation scale and multilingual setting: Experiments are restricted to training on small subsets of 6 languages at a time with limited data (~1 hour per language). A key appeal of multilingual models (like MMS and XLS-R) is scaling to tens or hundreds of languages concurrently. It remains unclear how CTC-DRO performs when scaled to dozens or hundreds of groups simultaneously.

Missing simple loss-normalization baselines: A common practical remedy for CTC length sensitivity is per-frame or per-label character normalization (e.g., dividing $L_{\text{CTC}}$ by output length $U$ or audio duration). While Section 3.2 mentions that initial experiments showed normalizing for transcript length was inadequate, quantitative baseline comparisons against standard DRO with normalized CTC loss are not provided.

Theoretical connection to DRO uncertainty sets: While the smoothed objective $\max_q \sum_g \log(q_g + \alpha) L_g$ is motivated intuitively and shown to recover group DRO as $\alpha \to \infty$, its interpretation as a distributionally robust objective over a well-defined uncertainty set is not formally established, functioning primarily as an empirical smoothing heuristic.

Checkpoint selection bias: The paper notes that model checkpoints for group DRO and CTC-DRO are selected based on the largest CER improvement on the worst-performing language on the development set. It is important to confirm whether the baseline model was selected on the same metric or on average validation loss/CER, as differing selection criteria could influence comparative outcomes.

strengths: Clear problem identification: The paper clearly identifies and illustrates a critical failure mode when applying group distributionally robust optimization (group DRO) to sequence tasks like speech recognition using CTC loss, namely that CTC loss scales with sequence duration and possesses irreducible linguistic variations that cause standard group DRO to destabilize and overfit to specific groups.

Effective and practical methodology: The proposed CTC-DRO method introduces two simple, computationally lightweight, and well-motivated techniques—duration-matched batching and a smoothed group weight update rule—that directly address the scaling and weight collapse issues.

Solid empirical results: Across 14 experimental configurations (5 language sets on both MMS and XLS-R, including balanced and unbalanced data regimes), CTC-DRO consistently and significantly outperforms both empirical risk minimization (baseline) and group DRO on worst-group CER (up to 65.9% relative reduction) while maintaining or improving average CER in 13 out of 14 cases.

Insightful analysis and ablations: The subtractive ablation study effectively isolates the individual impacts of duration matching and weight smoothing, and the group weight trajectories in Figure 2 clearly validate that CTC-DRO maintains stable and balanced group weights throughout training.
weaknesses: Limited comparison to standard multilingual and sequence heuristics: The paper compares primarily against standard empirical risk minimization and vanilla group DRO. It would be significantly strengthened by comparing against standard practical baselines, such as temperature-based multilingual data sampling (commonly used in multilingual ASR/LLMs), simple per-frame/per-token loss normalization of CTC, or other DRO variants designed to handle label/group noise (e.g., CVaR DRO or calibrated DRO).

Evaluation on small language subsets: While the experiments cover 5 diverse sets, each set only contains 6 languages trained on limited data (1 hour per language in the balanced setup). Real-world multilingual ASR models typically train on dozens or hundreds of languages simultaneously. In Algorithm 2, waiting until all groups have at least one batch processed before updating weights (line 11) may not scale trivially to regimes with 50-100+ groups.

Theoretical interpretation of the objective: The smoothed objective in Eq. (10) replaces the standard linear mixture $\sum_g q_g L_g$ with $\sum_g \log(q_g + \alpha) L_g$. While the resulting Hedge-style update has intuitive damping properties, the paper does not clarify the minimax or distributionally robust interpretation of this objective in terms of an uncertainty set or dual formulation over distributions.

Discrepancy in checkpoint selection: Section 4 notes that baselines are chosen based on the lowest loss on the development data, whereas CTC-DRO and group DRO checkpoints are selected based on the largest CER improvement on the worst-performing language relative to the baseline. Evaluating baselines under the same checkpoint selection metric would ensure an entirely fair comparison.

strengths: Addresses a well-known, important practical limitation: Group DRO fundamentally relies on the comparability of loss magnitudes across groups, which fails in sequence-level tasks like CTC-based speech recognition where loss scales with sequence duration and phonotactic/acoustic properties.

The proposed smoothing formulation of the Group DRO objective is simple, elegant, and leads to an intuitive Hedge-style update rule that penalizes runaway weight concentration without adding noticeable computational overhead.

Strong and consistent empirical improvements over both standard training and standard Group DRO across 5 different language sets and two competitive pre-trained architectures (XLS-R and MMS), successfully making DRO viable where prior work (e.g., Gao et al., 2022) observed degradation.

Informative analysis: The group weight progression plot (Figure 2) clearly illustrates the pathology of Group DRO (weight starvation and extreme oscillation) and how CTC-DRO stabilizes training dynamics, supported by clear component ablations (Table 4).
weaknesses: Scale of evaluation is relatively constrained: Experiments are limited to small subsets of 6 languages with 1 to ~9 hours of data per language. In modern multilingual ASR setups involving dozens or hundreds of languages, waiting for all groups to be sampled before performing a weight update (line 11 of Algorithm 2) may pose scalability and scheduling challenges.

Weakened connection to the minimax DRO framework: The standard Group DRO objective directly targets the minimax worst-case risk $\min_\theta \max_g \mathcal{R}_g(\theta)$. Replacing this with $\sum_g \log(q_g + \alpha) L_g$ departs from this minimax objective, and the manuscript does not provide theoretical characterization or robust generalization bounds for what objective is actually being solved at equilibrium.

Missing comparisons to standard length-normalization baselines: Standard ASR toolkits frequently employ token- or frame-normalized CTC loss (normalizing by transcription length $U$ or acoustic frames $D$) or loss-calibrated DRO variants (e.g., baseline subtraction as in Oren et al., 2019). The authors state in Section 3.2 that normalizing by transcript length did not resolve the issue in initial experiments, but empirical numbers comparing against length-normalized CTC baselines are not provided.

strengths: Identifies a clear and practically important failure mode of group distributionally robust optimization (group DRO) in multilingual speech recognition: CTC losses scale with utterance length and vary with intrinsic language difficulty, causing standard group DRO weights to degenerate onto high-loss groups.

Proposes a well-motivated, elegant, and computationally lightweight solution (CTC-DRO) combining input duration-matched batching and a mathematically grounded smoothed maximization objective over group weights that prevents weight collapse.

Provides extensive experimental validation across five distinct language subsets of ML-SUPERB 2.0 under both balanced and unbalanced data regimes, testing two prominent multilingual foundation models (MMS and XLS-R).

Presents thorough analytical experiments, including ablations of individual components, weight trajectory visualizations demonstrating optimization stability, comparisons against naive loss normalization (per-frame and per-token), and scaling tests up to 18 languages.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, clearly organized, and transparent about experimental choices, hyperparameter tuning, and compute requirements.
weaknesses: Experiments are conducted primarily on small subsets of 6 languages (and an extension to 18 languages in Appendix H) with limited training hours per language (1 to 9 hours), whereas modern massively multilingual ASR often scales to hundreds or thousands of languages simultaneously.

As shown in the multi-seed robustness analysis (Table 15, Set 3 XLS-R), gains on worst-language CER can be modest or within seed variance when the baseline performance gap between languages is already relatively small.

While CER is the primary target metric, the objective optimizes a smoothed function of the surrogate CTC loss, which can occasionally lead to slight mismatches between CTC loss minimization, character error rate (CER), and word error rate (WER) across languages.

strengths: Clear problem identification: The paper clearly identifies and analyzes a fundamental failure mode when applying group DRO to sequence-level tasks trained with the CTC loss—namely, that CTC losses scale with utterance length and vary with phonetic/acoustic characteristics, causing standard group DRO to disproportionately weight certain groups regardless of true downstream performance.

Principled and lightweight method: The proposed smoothed maximization objective (which maximizes $\sum_g \log(q_g + \alpha) L_g$) provides a theoretically sound update rule that discourages runaway weight concentration while preserving the core mechanism of robust optimization, incurring virtually zero extra computational overhead.

Thorough empirical evaluation: The method is tested across five diverse sets of languages under both balanced and unbalanced data conditions, using two distinct self-supervised speech foundation models (MMS and XLS-R), demonstrating consistent and significant reductions in worst-language CER (up to 47.1% relative reduction).

Detailed analysis and transparency: The authors provide comprehensive ablations dissecting the contributions of both the duration-matching batch sampler and the smoothing parameter $\alpha$, group weight trajectory visualizations demonstrating training stability, multi-seed experiments, and a scaling experiment up to 18 languages.
weaknesses: Scaling to very large language inventories: While the authors evaluate up to 18 languages in Appendix H, the relative improvements in worst-language CER diminish somewhat (around 8.9%–9.2% relative on balanced data) compared to the 6-language subsets, leaving open questions about scaling behavior in massive multilingual models (e.g., 50–100+ languages).

Sensitivity in low-margin settings: In the multi-seed evaluation (Table 15), for language set 3 with XLS-R, CTC-DRO yielded a slightly worse worst-case CER on 2 out of 4 seeds (average delta of -1.5%), indicating that when baseline disparities are small, the benefits of the robust weighting can be sensitive to initialization and optimization noise.

Tuning overhead for $\alpha$ and $\eta_q$: The introduction of $\alpha$ adds a critical hyperparameter that requires grid search alongside the group step size $\eta_q$, though the authors show that a relatively narrow search space ($\{0.1, 0.5, 1.0\}$) is sufficient.

strengths: Clear problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies and formalizes a critical failure mode of Group DRO in sequence modeling tasks trained with CTC loss, specifically showing how sequence length variation and irreducible loss disparities lead to pathological weight concentration.

Sound and principled methodology: The proposed CTC-DRO introduces two complementary and intuitive solutions—length-matched batch loss aggregation and a smoothed group-weight maximization objective ($\\sum_g \\log(q_g + \\alpha) L_g$). The mathematical derivation is clean and directly leads to a well-behaved update rule.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across two standard self-supervised speech foundation models (XLS-R and MMS) across five diverse 6-language subsets from the ML-SUPERB 2.0 benchmark, as well as an 18-language scaling setup, across both balanced and unbalanced data regimes.

Thorough analysis and ablations: The manuscript includes detailed ablations showing the necessity of both the length-matched batching and the smoothing parameter, empirical tracking of group weight trajectories that validate the hypothesis regarding GDRO weight collapse, multi-seed variance analyses, and experiments comparing against explicit loss normalization (per-frame / per-token).

High practical efficiency: CTC-DRO introduces almost negligible computational overhead (<1.5% wall-clock training time increase) while consistently reducing worst-case CER (by up to 47.1% relative) and frequently improving average CER without sacrificing language identification accuracy.
weaknesses: Modest data and language scale in primary setups: While typical multilingual ASR systems often cover dozens to hundreds of languages simultaneously, the primary experiments consider 6 languages at a time, with training limited to 1–9 hours per language. Although the authors provide an 18-language scaling experiment in Appendix H, evaluating larger-scale corpora (e.g., hundreds of hours per language) would further strengthen the practical impact.

Batch sampling dynamics: The fixed-duration batch sampler creates batches with differing numbers of utterances depending on average sample length. While this matches total duration, it causes variance in the effective batch size (number of sequences) per group update, which is not deeply analyzed in terms of gradient variance.

Marginal degradation in specific low-disparity cases: On setups where baseline performance was already relatively balanced across languages (such as Set 3 in Table 15 for XLS-R), CTC-DRO can slightly underperform ERM baselines on the worst group, indicating that the choice of tuning $\\alpha$ and $\\eta_q$ is sensitive to the intrinsic variance between groups.
